headline: High-risk shared filesystem and broad egress make prompt injection, leakage, and cascading errors plausible; compliance risk is moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Windsurf reads and writes workspace files and uses MCP/clipboard, while xonsh reads filesystem contents and executes shell commands. That creates a plausible content-to-command bridge where attacker-controlled files or copied text from Windsurf can influence xonsh. The shared local filesystem makes this interaction default, not unusual.
conditions: IF Windsurf writes attacker-controlled instructions into a shared workspace file, xonsh can ingest them as shell input.
IF clipboard copy-paste is used between the two agents, prompt-like text can cross the boundary without provenance checks.
mitigations: Disable clipboard bridging between agents.
Use separate workspaces or per-agent directories.
Require manual review of any file content before xonsh executes it.
Turn off MCP access for Windsurf unless needed.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for shared files.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents touch source code and filesystem contents, and Windsurf explicitly shares state with other instances via the local filesystem. xonsh also reads environment variables and filesystem contents. This makes accidental exposure of open files, configs, or secrets plausible in default workspace-sharing setups, even though neither profile shows automatic secret exfiltration by itself.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same local workspace, files opened by Windsurf can be read by xonsh.
IF sensitive values are present in environment variables or config files, xonsh can access them from the shared filesystem or shell context.
mitigations: Separate sensitive files into a non-shared directory.
Unset secrets from the shell environment before launching xonsh.
Restrict Windsurf to a read-only clone for sensitive projects.
Review workspace permissions for both agents.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Windsurf can write the filesystem, modify git state, execute shell, and use MCP; xonsh can also execute shell and write the filesystem. Because Windsurf shares state via the local filesystem and both can mutate the same workspace, concurrent edits and git-state races are plausible by default. The lack of locking in either profile makes conflict risk high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory, file overwrites or partial writes can occur.
IF both agents modify the same git repository without external locking, branch or index conflicts can occur.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working tree.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Use git locks or a single committer workflow.
Limit Windsurf auto-execute for commands touching shared files.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Windsurf can generate code and act through shell/MCP, while xonsh can execute shell commands and manipulate files. If xonsh consumes Windsurf-produced output as authoritative, mistakes can cascade into real actions or commits. Because both agents have action-taking authority and no verification channel is documented, the default pathway is dangerous.
conditions: IF xonsh executes commands emitted by Windsurf without review, incorrect instructions can become system actions.
IF Windsurf-generated code is piped into xonsh scripts, errors can propagate into files or repositories.
mitigations: Require human approval before executing cross-agent output.
Insert a validation step between Windsurf and xonsh.
Use dry-run mode for any generated commands.
Log and diff all proposed changes before execution.
requires-engineering: build a verifier agent or policy gate.

E_compliance.rationale: Windsurf is a closed-source editor agent with broad network egress and BYOK model-provider keys, while xonsh is open-source and isolated but can access filesystem contents and environment variables. The pair can therefore move the same data class through different retention and processing regimes, creating a compliance mismatch risk. No specific residency or certification gap is documented, so this stays medium.
conditions: IF regulated data is edited in the shared workspace, Windsurf may transmit it through its model proxy or MCP-connected services.
IF organizational policy requires uniform retention or residency controls, the differing agent architectures can violate it.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared workspace.
Disable network egress for Windsurf on regulated projects.
Review vendor terms for both tools before use.
Separate compliant and non-compliant projects by workspace.
requires-engineering: implement data-loss-prevention controls.
